chapters.1.summary: The LORD speaks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting about offerings. A burnt offering from the herd must be a male without defect. The giver lays a hand on its head and kills it. The priests sprinkle its blood on the altar and arrange the pieces on the fire. The giver washes the inner parts and legs, and the priest burns all of it. The same steps apply to a sheep or goat. A burnt offering may also be doves or pigeons, which the priest handles. Each is called a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
chapters.1.lds: The giver lays a hand on the animal’s head (verse 4). What does the verse say the offering does for him?
chapters.2.summary: A meal offering is fine flour with oil and frankincense. The priest burns a handful with all the frankincense as a memorial part. The rest belongs to Aaron and his sons and is most holy. The offering may be baked in an oven, on a griddle, or in a pan. It must have no yeast and no honey. Every meal offering must be seasoned with salt. A first fruits offering is fresh grain, roasted and crushed, with oil and frankincense.
chapters.2.lds: Only a handful of the flour is burned (verse 2). Who receives the rest in verse 3?
chapters.3.summary: A peace offering may be a male or female animal without defect. It may come from the herd, the sheep, or the goats. The giver lays a hand on its head and kills it at the tent door. The priests sprinkle the blood around the altar. The fat around the inner parts, the kidneys, and the liver cover are burned. For a lamb, the whole fat tail is burned too. All the fat belongs to the LORD. Israel must never eat fat or blood.
chapters.3.lds: The peace offering ends with a rule for every home (verse 17). What two things may Israel never eat?
chapters.4.summary: These offerings are for sins done without meaning to. If the anointed priest sins, the people share the guilt, and he offers a bull. Its blood is sprinkled before the veil, and its body is burned outside the camp. If the whole assembly sins, the elders lay hands on a bull. A ruler who sins brings a male goat. A common person brings a female goat or lamb. In each case the priest makes atonement, and the person is forgiven.
chapters.4.lds: The priest’s sin brings guilt “on the people” (verse 3). How does his offering compare with a common person’s in verse 28?
chapters.5.summary: Some cases need a trespass offering. A witness stays silent, a person touches something unclean, or someone swears a rash oath. The guilty person must confess the sin. He brings a female lamb or goat, and the priest makes atonement. If he cannot afford a lamb, he brings two doves or pigeons. If he cannot afford birds, he brings a tenth of an ephah of flour. One who misuses holy things brings a ram, repays the loss, and adds a fifth. A person who sins without knowing it is still guilty and brings a ram.
chapters.5.lds: Someone who cannot afford a lamb may bring birds or flour (verses 7, 11). What does the priest still do for him in verse 13?
chapters.6.summary: A person may cheat a neighbor over a deposit, a theft, or a found item. He must return it in full and add a fifth. He gives it to the owner on the day he is found guilty. Then he brings a ram as a trespass offering and is forgiven. The priests must keep the altar fire burning all night and clear the ashes. The priests eat what is left of the meal offering in a holy place. A priest’s own meal offering is burned whole. The priest who offers a sin offering eats it in the court.
chapters.6.lds: The wrongdoer pays the neighbor back and adds a fifth (verse 5). Which comes first in verses 5–6, the repayment or the offering?
chapters.7.summary: The trespass offering is most holy, and the priests eat it in a holy place. The priest who offers a burnt offering keeps its skin. A peace offering for thanksgiving comes with cakes and bread. Its meat must be eaten the same day. Meat from a vow or free will offering may be eaten for two days. Anything left on the third day is burned. No one may eat fat or blood, and the unclean may not eat this meat. The breast and right thigh of peace offerings go to the priests.
chapters.7.lds: Thanksgiving meat must be eaten that day (verse 15). What does that rule do with a whole animal’s worth of food?
chapters.8.summary: The LORD tells Moses to gather all the people at the tent door. Moses washes Aaron and his sons before them. He dresses Aaron in the tunic, robe, ephod, breastplate, and turban. He anoints the tabernacle, the altar, and Aaron with oil. He offers a bull for sin and a ram as a burnt offering. He puts blood from a second ram on their right ears, thumbs, and big toes. He sprinkles oil and blood on them and their garments. They stay at the tent door seven days.
chapters.8.lds: The Church manual connects priestly service with sacred preparation. Who is called to watch Aaron’s appointment (verses 3–4)?
chapters.9.summary: On the eighth day Moses tells Aaron to offer a calf for his own sin. The people bring a goat, a calf, a lamb, a bull, and a ram. Moses says the LORD’s glory will appear to them. Aaron first offers the sin offering and burnt offering for himself. Then he offers the people’s goat, burnt offering, meal offering, and peace offerings. He lifts his hands and blesses the people. Moses and Aaron go into the tent, come out, and bless them again. The LORD’s glory appears, fire burns the offering, and the people fall down.
chapters.9.lds: Aaron must make atonement “for yourself, and for the people” (verse 7). Whose offering does he make first in verse 8?
chapters.10.summary: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire that the LORD did not command. Fire comes out from the LORD and kills them. Moses says God will be shown holy, and Aaron keeps silent. Cousins carry the bodies out of the camp. Aaron and his other sons may not mourn openly or leave the tent. The LORD tells Aaron that priests must not drink wine on duty. They must tell holy from common and teach Israel the laws. Moses is angry that the sin offering was burned, not eaten, and accepts Aaron’s answer.
chapters.10.lds: The Church manual discusses responsibility in sacred service. Aaron explains why he did not eat the offering (verse 19). How does Moses respond in verse 20?
chapters.11.summary: The LORD tells Moses and Aaron which animals Israel may eat. Land animals must have a split hoof and chew the cud. Camels, hyraxes, hares, and pigs are unclean. Water creatures must have fins and scales. Many named birds are forbidden, and so are most winged insects, except locusts and grasshoppers. Touching a dead unclean animal makes a person unclean until evening. Pots and ovens that touch a carcass must be washed or broken. Israel must be holy, because the LORD who brought them from Egypt is holy.
chapters.11.lds: The Church manual studies these rules within Israel’s covenant. A person who carries a carcass is unclean “until the evening” (verse 40). What must that person do?
chapters.12.summary: A woman who bears a son is unclean for seven days. The boy is circumcised on the eighth day. She then waits thirty-three more days and may not enter the sanctuary. For a daughter the times are doubled: two weeks and sixty-six days. When the time ends, she brings the priest a lamb and a pigeon or dove. If she cannot afford a lamb, she brings two doves or two pigeons. The priest makes atonement for her, and she is clean.
chapters.12.lds: A mother who cannot afford a lamb may bring two birds (verse 8). What result does the verse promise her?
chapters.15.summary: A man with a bodily discharge is unclean. His bed, his seat, and anyone he touches become unclean until evening. When it stops, he counts seven days, washes, and brings two birds to the priest. A man with an emission of semen bathes and is unclean until evening. A woman in her monthly period is unclean for seven days. A longer flow of blood makes her unclean for as long as it lasts. When it stops, she counts seven days and brings two birds. These rules keep Israel from defiling the tabernacle that is among them.
chapters.15.lds: Verse 31 gives the reason for these rules. What is it?
chapters.13.summary: A person with a swelling, scab, or bright spot goes to a priest. The priest looks for white hair and a mark deeper than the skin. If it is unclear, he isolates the person for seven days and looks again. He may wait seven more days before deciding. A faded mark means clean, and a spreading one means unclean. A person with leprosy wears torn clothes, calls out “Unclean,” and lives outside the camp. Cloth or leather with a greenish or reddish spot is also shown to the priest. It is shut away seven days and burned if the spot spreads.
chapters.13.lds: The priest waits seven days, then seven more, before he decides (verses 4–5). How can a community care for people who must stay apart?
chapters.14.summary: This is the law for a healed leper. The priest goes outside the camp to examine him. Two birds are used: one is killed, and the living one is set free. The person washes, shaves, and waits seven days before entering his tent. On the eighth day he brings lambs, flour, and oil, and the priest makes atonement. A poor person may bring one lamb and two birds. A house with spreading mildew is emptied, shut up, scraped, and, if needed, torn down. A house that stays clear is declared clean.
chapters.14.lds: A poor person brings “such as he is able to afford” (verse 22). How does the chapter help someone return to the community?
chapters.16.summary: Aaron may not enter the Most Holy Place at just any time. Once a year he bathes and dresses in plain linen. He offers a bull for himself and his house. He casts lots over two goats: one for the LORD and one as the scapegoat. He takes incense and blood inside the veil and sprinkles the mercy seat. He makes atonement for the Holy Place, the tent, and the altar. He confesses Israel’s sins over the live goat and sends it into the wilderness. On that day, the tenth of the seventh month, all Israel rests and humbles itself.
chapters.16.lds: The older Church manual connects the Day of Atonement with Christ’s work to forgive sin. Verse 16 says the tent dwells “in the middle of their uncleanness.” What is cleansed on this day besides the people?
chapters.17.summary: Anyone who kills a bull, lamb, or goat must bring it to the tent door. Killing it elsewhere counts as bloodshed. The rule is meant to end sacrifices in the open field to goat idols. The priest sprinkles the blood on the LORD’s altar. No Israelite or foreigner living among them may eat blood. The life is in the blood, and God gave it for atonement on the altar. A hunter must pour out the blood of his catch and cover it with dust. Anyone who eats an animal found dead must wash and wait until evening.
chapters.17.lds: Verse 11 says “the life of the flesh is in the blood.” What must a hunter do with an animal’s blood in verse 13?
chapters.18.summary: The LORD tells Israel not to follow the practices of Egypt or Canaan. They must keep his statutes and live by them. The chapter forbids sexual relations with close relatives, and it lists them one by one. It forbids marrying a wife’s sister as a rival, and adultery. It forbids giving children to Molech. It forbids a man lying with a man, and sex with animals. The nations before Israel did these things, and the land was defiled. The land vomited them out, and it will do the same to Israel.
chapters.18.lds: Verse 28 warns that the land can “vomit you out also.” Whom do the rules in verses 6–18 protect inside a household?
chapters.19.summary: The LORD tells all Israel to be holy, because he is holy. They must respect parents, keep Sabbaths, and avoid idols. Farmers must leave field corners and fallen grapes for the poor and the foreigner. They must not steal, lie, hold back wages overnight, or trip the blind. Judges must not favor the poor or the great. They must not hate or take revenge, but love their neighbor as themselves. They must love the foreigner as themselves, since they were foreigners in Egypt. Scales, weights, and measures must be honest.
chapters.19.lds: How can love change the way you treat workers and strangers? Verse 36 requires honest weights. What does verse 13 require for a hired worker’s pay?
chapters.20.summary: Anyone who gives a child to Molech must be stoned. If the people look away, God will act against that family. Those who turn to mediums are cut off. Israel must be holy and keep God’s statutes. Death is set for cursing parents, adultery, and several unions forbidden in chapter 18. Other unions bring being cut off or dying childless. Israel must not follow the customs of the nations being driven out. The LORD has set them apart to be his and to inherit the land.
chapters.20.lds: Consider moral responsibility while keeping ancient civil penalties distinct from present Church practice. The LORD says he has “separated you from the peoples” (verse 24). What promise comes with that in the same verse?
chapters.21.summary: Priests may not touch the dead, except for their closest relatives. They may not shave their heads or cut their flesh. They may not marry a prostitute or a divorced woman. The high priest may not go near any dead body, even a parent’s. He must marry a virgin of his own people. A priest with a bodily defect may not come near the altar or the veil. The list includes the blind, the lame, and the injured. He may still eat the holy and most holy food.
chapters.21.lds: What duties come with service in a holy place? A priest with a defect may not serve at the altar (verse 21). What does verse 22 still give him?
chapters.22.summary: Priests must stay away from the holy food while they are unclean. An unclean priest washes, waits until evening, and then may eat his bread. Only the priest’s household may eat it, including a slave he bought. A married daughter may not, but a childless widow who returns home may. Anyone who eats it by mistake repays it and adds a fifth. Animals for vows and free gifts must have no defect. A newborn animal stays seven days with its mother. A cow or ewe and its young may not be killed on the same day.
chapters.22.lds: An animal and its young may not be killed on one day (verse 28). What does verse 27 require for a newborn animal?
chapters.23.summary: The LORD gives Moses the set feasts of the year. The Sabbath comes every seventh day. Passover falls in the first month, with seven days of unleavened bread. A sheaf of first grain is waved, and fifty days later two loaves are offered. At harvest the field corners and gleanings are left for the poor and the foreigner. The seventh month has a day of trumpets and the day of atonement. Then comes the seven-day feast of booths. Israel lives in shelters to remember the journey out of Egypt.
chapters.23.lds: A harvest rule sits in the middle of the feast list (verse 22). Whom does it provide for?
chapters.24.summary: Israel must bring pure olive oil so the lamp burns every night. Twelve loaves are set on the gold table each Sabbath, and the priests eat them. Then a fight breaks out in the camp. A man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father curses the Name. He is held until the LORD’s will is known. The LORD orders the hearers to lay hands on him and all to stone him. The LORD adds rules: life for life, eye for eye, and payment for animals. The same law applies to the foreigner and the native-born.
chapters.24.lds: How can our words honor God? Verse 22 says one law covers the foreigner and the native-born. Why does that matter in this case (verses 10–11)?
chapters.25.summary: Every seventh year the land must rest, with no sowing or pruning. After forty-nine years a trumpet announces the fiftieth year, the Jubilee. Liberty is declared, and each person returns to his family’s land. Land prices follow the number of crops left before the Jubilee. The land may not be sold forever, because it belongs to the LORD. A relative may buy back land for a poor brother. Israel must lend to the poor without interest. A poor Israelite who sells himself serves as hired help until the Jubilee.
chapters.25.lds: The LORD says, “The land is mine” (verse 23). What does that mean for a family that had to sell its field?
chapters.26.summary: Israel must make no idols and must keep the Sabbaths. If they obey, God will send rain, harvests, peace, and victory. He will set his tent among them and walk with them. If they refuse, he will send sickness, defeat, drought, wild animals, and siege. Each stage is harder than the last. In the end their cities fall, and they are scattered among the nations. Then the land will enjoy the Sabbaths it missed. If they confess, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham.
chapters.26.lds: What hope remains after the warnings? In verse 44 God says he will not reject his people in exile. What will he remember in verse 45?
chapters.27.summary: A person vowed to the LORD is given a value in silver. The value depends on age and sex, from three to fifty shekels. A poor person is valued by the priest according to what he can pay. An animal given for offering becomes holy and may not be swapped. A house or field may be dedicated and bought back by adding a fifth. A field’s value is counted by the years left until the Jubilee. Firstborn animals already belong to the LORD. A tenth of crops and herds is holy to the LORD.
chapters.27.lds: A person too poor for the set value goes to the priest (verse 8). How does the priest decide the amount?
